title: Psalm 100: Enter His Gates with Thanksgiving
summary: In five verses the whole earth is called to shout to the LORD, serve him gladly, and come before him with singing. The reason is that the LORD is God, he made us, and we are his people and the sheep of his pasture. Worshipers are invited through the temple gates with thanks and praise, because the LORD is good, his loving devotion endures forever, and his faithfulness lasts through every generation.
story: Psalm 100 closes the group of kingship psalms that runs from Psalm 93 to here (with Psalm 94 as an interlude). It gathers their themes into a short doxology: the invitation to all the earth from Psalms 96 and 98, the shepherd language and the call to enter his presence from Psalm 95. Psalm 95 paired its invitation with a warning; Psalm 100 has no warning at all, only welcome. In the larger movement of Book IV, which answers the loss of David's throne by confessing the LORD as King, this psalm is the joyful summary before Psalm 101 turns to what a human king under God should be like.
historical:
The heading reads “A Psalm of thanksgiving”, and the Hebrew word todah can mean either thanksgiving in general or the thank offering, a sacrifice brought to the temple to give thanks for a rescue or a blessing (Leviticus 7:11-15). Some scholars think the psalm was sung as worshipers brought that offering through the gates into the temple courts; others read the heading more broadly, as a label for a song of praise. The psalm names no author and no event, and its date cannot be fixed. It assumes the temple in Jerusalem with its gates and courts, which could mean Solomon's temple or the one rebuilt after the exile.

There is a small but famous textual question in verse 3. The Hebrew consonants can be read as saying that he made us and not we ourselves, which is how the King James Version took it, or, with a word that sounds identical but is spelled differently, as “and we are His”. Jewish scribes noted the second reading in the margin, and most modern translations, including the Berean Standard Bible, follow it. Both readings make the same basic point: we did not make ourselves.
cultural:
Temple worship in Israel was a physical approach. Pilgrims came up to Jerusalem, passed through the outer gates, and entered courts that grew more restricted the closer they came to the sanctuary. To “enter His gates with thanksgiving” (verse 4) was to walk that route singing. The verb “serve” in verse 2 is the same word used for a servant's work and for worship; in the ancient world, a people served its king by labor and tribute, and this people serves its King with gladness.

The shepherd image was royal across the region, since kings called themselves shepherds of their people, but it was also plain daily life. A flock belonged to its owner, who marked it, pastured it, and protected it. To call Israel “the sheep of His pasture” (verse 3) was to say whose they were and who was responsible for them. Addressing “all the earth” (verse 1) extends that belonging, at least in invitation, to everyone.
literary: The psalm has two matching halves, each made of a call to worship followed by a reason. Verses 1 and 2 give three commands (make a joyful noise, serve, come), and verse 3 gives the reason: the LORD is God, he made us, we are his. Verse 4 gives three commands (enter, give thanks, bless), and verse 5 gives the reason: he is good, his love endures, his faithfulness continues. The command at the center, “Know that the LORD is God”, is the hinge. The final verse uses one of Israel's oldest confessions, the refrain that the LORD is good and his loving devotion endures forever, sung at great moments in the history books (2 Chronicles 5:13; Ezra 3:11).

outline.t: Come before him, for the LORD made us and we are his
Enter his gates, for the LORD is good and faithful

doctrines.note: Everything turns on “Know that the LORD is God”. Worship begins by recognizing who God is: the maker and owner of his people, good, loving, and faithful across generations.
“It is He who made us” grounds human belonging in creation. We are not self-made, and the right response to being made is gratitude.
God's people are “His people, and the sheep of His pasture” (verse 3), a flock with an owner and shepherd, gathered to worship together, and the psalm opens that gathering to all the earth.

words.note: Todah, thanksgiving or thank offering. It combines gratitude and confession: to give thanks in Israel meant telling publicly what God had done. The word appears in the heading and in verse 4, framing the psalm.

Avad, to serve or work. The same verb describes slave labor in Egypt (Exodus 1:13-14) and Israel's worship of God (Exodus 3:12). Serving the LORD with gladness recasts the language of bondage as joyful loyalty.

Yada, to know. In the Old Testament knowing is more than holding information; it means acknowledging and living in light of what is true, often in a relationship. To know that the LORD is God is to take him as one's own God.
Chesed, loving devotion, the steadfast love that keeps covenant. The psalm says it endures forever, which is the reason for the whole song: God's goodness is not a passing mood.

christ: Jesus calls himself the good shepherd who knows his sheep and lays down his life for them, and says he has other sheep, not of this fold, that he must bring so that there will be one flock (John 10:14-16). That picks up this psalm's two ideas, God's people as his flock and the invitation to all the earth. The New Testament also describes believers as having access to God's presence, entering through Christ with confidence (Hebrews 10:19-22), which Christians have read as the fulfillment of the psalm's call to enter his gates. The link is thematic; the psalm itself speaks of Israel's temple worship. The church has sung it for centuries, including in the sixteenth-century metrical version set to the tune still called Old Hundredth.
questions: The psalm commands gladness. Can joy be commanded, and if so, what does obeying that command look like on an ordinary day?
How does it change your sense of yourself to say “It is He who made us, and we are His” rather than to think of yourself as self-made?
Which generation before you passed God's faithfulness on to you, and how are you passing it on?
